bio_md:
# 孺子婴 · 主要事迹

刘婴是宣帝玄孙，[[han-ping-di|平帝]]崩后，[[xin-wang-mang|王莽]]立年仅二岁的刘婴为皇太子，号「孺子」，自己以周公自居，居摄践祚，称「假皇帝」——西汉名义上的最后一个皇帝，连正式即位都没有，便成了禅让大戏的道具。

居摄三年间，反对者并未绝迹：居摄二年，东郡太守翟义起兵讨莽，声势震动关东，旋被讨平。莽一面以武力镇压，一面加紧造势——初始元年，符命祥瑞与劝进表章如雪片般飞向长安，王莽终于在始建国元年废孺子为定安公，称帝改国号为新，西汉至此正式灭亡。

被废后的刘婴被幽闭禁锢，年岁渐长却不通人语；更始年间天下大乱，婴死于乱兵。他是中国帝制史上最年幼、最彻底的傀儡之一：两岁受命，四岁失国，一生从未真正拥有过任何权力，却偏偏以「皇帝」之名被写进史书。图鉴以「准帝」立页，附于王莽禅代与[[e-han-guangwu|光武中兴]]两端之间，正可作汉祚兴亡的注脚。

> 参考：点校本《汉书》卷099《王莽传》、《后汉书·刘玄传》，谭图第 2 册。

bio_parts_en.value: Liu Ying was a great-great-grandson of Emperor Xuan. After

raised the two-year-old Ying as heir apparent, styled "the Infant," casting himself as the Duke of Zhou and taking the regency in the infant's place, calling himself "Acting Emperor" — the nominal last emperor of Western Han, who was never even formally enthroned, became the prop of an abdication drama.

The three regency years were not without opposition: in the second Jushe year, Zhai Yi, governor of Dongjun, rose against Mang with an army that shook the lands east of the passes before being suppressed. Mang answered force with force and momentum with theater — in the first Chushi year, omens and petitions urging abdication flew into Chang'an like snow; in the first Shijianguo year he demoted the Infant to Duke of Ding'an, proclaimed himself emperor, and changed the dynasty's name to Xin. Western Han was formally finished.

The deposed Infant was shut away, and as he grew he could not even speak coherently; during the Gengshi era, amid the collapse of the Xin dynasty, he died in the disorder of the soldiery. He is among the youngest and most complete puppets in Chinese imperial history: invested at two, losing the state at four, never holding a scrap of power, yet written into the histories under the title of emperor. This gazetteer lists him as a quasi-emperor, standing between Mang's usurpation and the restoration of

— a footnote to the rise and fall of the Han mandate.

> References: the punctuated critical edition of the *Hanshu*, ch. 99 (Biography of Wang Mang), and the *Hou Hanshu*, biography of Liu Xuan; Tan Qixiang's atlas, vol. 2.
